Growth trajectories of Diapterus rhombeus suggest that individuals reach a maximum adult body length of 18 cm [Li = 18 cm], a value considerably smaller than the 42.3 cm figure occasionally cited for the species in outdated compilations. This more modest estimate is supported by the corresponding maximum adult wet weight of 76.45 grams [Wwi = 76.45 grams], derived from length-weight regressions based on local specimens. The field-collected data indicate that sexual maturation is initiated when fish attain a standard length at puberty of 13 cm [Lp = 13 cm], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 28.5 grams [Wwp = 28.5 grams]. This transition into reproductive maturity occurs after a period of substantial somatic investment, leaving approximately five centimeters of potential growth between the pubertal and ultimate body sizes. Such a pattern suggests that the species channels considerable energy toward continued somatic expansion even after the onset of gonadal activity, a life-history strategy observed in several iteroparous gerreids inhabiting similar tropical estuarine environments.

Reproductive output in Diapterus rhombeus has been quantified through fecundity analyses of gravid females captured during the peak spawning season. At a stable water temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], individuals produce approximately 712 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 712 eggs per day], a daily rate that represents the maximum reproductive capacity observed under favorable environmental conditions. This estimate was derived from whole-ovary counts of hydrated oocytes in females near the ultimate body length and reflects the species' considerable fecundity relative to its modest adult size. The high daily egg production is characteristic of batch-spawning teleosts that release multiple cohorts of oocytes over an extended breeding period, thereby maximizing lifetime reproductive success in the variable conditions of coastal lagoons. Field observations confirm that spawning events occur regularly throughout the warmer months when thermal conditions are optimal for embryonic development and larval survival, ensuring that the reproductive window is fully exploited.

Examination of recently spawned eggs and early developmental stages provides critical data on initial offspring size in Diapterus rhombeus. Based on a mean egg diameter of 0.42 millimeters, the estimated wet weight at birth for a newly fertilized ovum is 0.000039 grams [Wwb = 0.000039 grams], a value calculated from the volumetric formula for a sphere. This minute initial mass places the species among the small-egged gerreids, an adaptation that promotes high fecundity at the expense of per-offspring investment. Following external fertilization and subsequent incubation within the pelagic zone, the transparent, yolk-laden eggs drift with currents before hatching into yolk-sac larvae that are entirely endotrophic during their initial days. The limited yolk reserves must sustain the prolarvae until the point of no return when mouth opening and retinal differentiation permit first exogenous feeding, a critical transitional period that strongly influences early survival rates in the planktonic environment.

Longevity records for Diapterus rhombeus indicate that the species exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 8.5 years [am = approximately 8.5 years] at 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C] under natural conditions in the wild, based on otolith-based age estimates from populations inhabiting western Atlantic coastal systems. This extended lifespan is consistent with the moderately paced life-history strategy typical of many gerreid fishes that occupy stable, productive nursery grounds. The analysis of sagittal otolith annuli from a sample of over two hundred individuals revealed that the oldest specimen captured was a female measuring 17.8 centimeters in standard length, approaching the asymptotic size limit. Such longevity allows for multiple reproductive seasons, with iteroparous spawning occurring annually after the onset of sexual maturity. The combination of a long reproductive lifespan and high daily fecundity suggests that the species compensates for small offspring size through repeated, large-volume spawning events, a demographic strategy that buffers against variable recruitment success.

Comparative analysis of body size and age data across Gerreidae places Diapterus rhombeus at the smaller end of the size spectrum within the genus, with an asymptotic length notably lower than that of congeners such as Diapterus auratus. The ultimate wet weight of 76.45 grams [Wwi = 76.45 grams] and the wet weight at puberty of 28.5 grams [Wwp = 28.5 grams] together indicate that females invest roughly 37 percent of their asymptotic mass before initiating reproduction, a proportional investment that aligns with predictions for species inhabiting productive estuarine environments.
